summary: This is a replication of the Bigoni et al. (2012) cartel laboratory experiment, run with LLM pricing agents (Claude Haiku 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5) in place of human students, using the same payoffs, enforcement regimes (laissez-faire, fine, leniency, reward) and matching rules, so that every result can be compared directly with the human data. The open harness lets anyone, for example a competition authority, test any pricing model against fines, leniency and whistleblower rewards before such agents reach real markets, and it comes with pre-registration, scripted and placebo controls and a contamination check. It shows that Haiku forms cartels as often as humans when nothing is prohibited but holds them near the monopoly price because it almost never undercuts, that told-only fines, leniency and rewards deter it far more than they deterred people, and that Sonnet forms no explicit cartels under any prohibition yet still keeps prices above the competitive level without talking; only 2 of the 7 tested human results reproduce.
main_claim: Told-only fines, leniency and reward rules deter explicit cartels among LLM pricing agents much more than they deterred human subjects, but the cartels that do survive keep the monopoly price, and one model keeps prices supracompetitive with no communication at all, which these instruments cannot reach.
who_should_care: Competition authorities and antitrust researchers who rely on leniency and whistleblower programmes and need to know whether those tools still work once LLM agents set prices.
what_is_not_proven: Nothing is shown for real markets, real money, other model providers or later model versions, or the agents' actual reasoning, because the game is a stylised lab setup with told-only point penalties, tested on two Claude models at a single date with only four independent pool sessions per regime.
